claims.source: Suppression of either population starting at the third larval instar results in severe pupal ecdysis deficits and lethality in 100% of animals (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Blocking activity in CCAP-R-expressing neurons starting at the third larval instar results in severe pupal ecdysis deficits and lethality in 100% of animals.
claims.source: Suppression of either population starting at the third larval instar results in severe pupal ecdysis deficits and lethality in 100% of animals (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Animals in which the Rk-expressing neurons are suppressed lack all movement and therefore all phases of the pupal ecdysis sequence.
claims.source: Animals in which the Rk-expressing neurons are suppressed are most impaired, lacking all movement and therefore all phases of the pupal ecdysis sequence (Figure 2C, top; Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Video 3.

claims.claim: Pupal development in animals with suppressed Rk-expressing neurons is otherwise normal: a bubble appears in the abdomen and the fat body degrades on schedule.
claims.source: Interestingly, pupal development in these animals is otherwise normal: a bubble appears in the abdomen (Figure 2B, left, arrow) and the fat body degrades on schedule, but the overt gut movements that herald the onset of Phase I behaviors (Robertson, 1936) fail to appear.
claims.evidence: This is supported by observations shown in Figure 2B and a citation to Robertson, 1936.

claims.claim: Animals with suppressed Rk-expressing neurons remain viable for many hours despite not initiating pupal ecdysis.
claims.source: The presence of a sustained heartbeat throughout indicates that the animals remain viable for many hours, despite not initiating pupal ecdysis.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claims.claim: Animals in which the CCAP-R neurons are suppressed execute only a mixture of weak and irregular contractions during a period of abdominal lifting with some resemblance to Phase I.
claims.source: Animals in which the CCAP-R neurons are suppressed also lack normal ecdysis behavior, executing only a mixture of weak and irregular contractions during a period of abdominal lifting with some resemblance to Phase I (Figure 2C, bottom; Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Video 3.

claims.claim: The two distinct groups of neurons targeted by Bursicon and CCAP are both essential for pupal ecdysis.
claims.source: We conclude that the two distinct groups of neurons targeted by Bursicon and CCAP are both essential for pupal ecdysis.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the suppression experiments showing severe deficits.

claims.claim: Rk is not expressed in motor neurons.
claims.source: We observed expression in only a handful of neurons of the thoracic ganglia, none of which extend axons to muscles, indicating that Rk is not expressed in motor neurons (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by intersectional labeling data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Rk is not highly expressed in neurons that receive the hormonal input that initiates the ecdysis sequence.
claims.source: We likewise find that Rk is not highly expressed in neurons that receive the hormonal input that initiates the ecdysis sequence as determined using a Rk hemidriver in conjunction with ETHRA and ETHRB hemidrivers to identify neurons that co-express Rk and either the A- or B-isoform of the ETHR (Figure 3A', A", Diao et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by intersectional labeling data shown in Figure 3A' and A".

claims.claim: Only a small number of neurons co-express Rk and either ETHRA or ETHRB.
claims.source: For both isoforms, only a small number of neurons was identified that co-expressed Rk, and the suppression of these neurons with 2X UAS-Kir2.1 failed to block pupal ecdysis (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data (not shown).

claims.claim: The Rk-expressing neurons essential for pupal ecdysis do not belong to either the input or the output layers of the ecdysis network.
claims.source: The Rk-expressing neurons essential for pupal ecdysis thus do not belong to either the input or the output layers of the ecdysis network and must therefore occupy an intermediate position in the circuit hierarchy.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the intersectional labeling data showing Rk is not in motor neurons or ETHR neurons.

claims.claim: The alternating oscillations in VNC-Rk neurons were sustained for 9 min on average and consisted of 15 cycles of oscillation.
claims.source: Quantifying the alternating oscillations, we found that the midline oscillations were, on average, sustained for 9 min. and consisted of 15 cycles of oscillation.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of Ca++ imaging data.

claims.claim: The pattern of VNC-Rk neuron activity induced by ATP is reminiscent of the Phase II swinging motor program.
claims.source: This striking pattern of activity was reminiscent of the Phase II swinging motor program, which is likewise induced by activation of neurons that express Bursicon and, as shown by muscle Ca++ imaging below (Figure 4C), consists of approximately 18 bouts of alternating left-right abdominal swinging and lasts approximately 17 min.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of neuronal activity patterns with behavioral patterns.

claims.claim: Phase II consists of approximately 18 bouts of alternating left-right abdominal swinging and lasts approximately 17 min.
claims.source: This striking pattern of activity was reminiscent of the Phase II swinging motor program, which is likewise induced by activation of neurons that express Bursicon and, as shown by muscle Ca++ imaging below (Figure 4C), consists of approximately 18 bouts of alternating left-right abdominal swinging and lasts approximately 17 min.
claims.evidence: This is supported by muscle Ca++ imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The induced activity of the Rk-expressing neurons in the isolated nervous system appears to be correlated with the motor output induced by a similar stimulus in the intact animal.
claims.source: The induced activity of the Rk-expressing neurons in the isolated nervous system thus appears to be correlated with the motor output induced by a similar stimulus in the intact animal.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the similarity in activity patterns and durations.

claims.claim: Exposure of excised pupal nervous systems to ETH1 stimulates a fictive pupal ecdysis sequence.
claims.source: We took advantage of the fact that exposure of excised pupal nervous systems to the ETH peptide, ETH1, stimulates a fictive pupal ecdysis sequence (Diao et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2006; Mena et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Diao et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2006; Mena et al., 2016.

claims.claim: In excised CNS preparations treated with ETH1, VNC-Rk neurons show enhanced Ca++ activity relative to preparations that did not receive ETH1.
claims.source: We monitored UAS-GCaMP6s activity in the VNC-Rk neurons as before and found that in excised CNS preparations treated with ETH1 these neurons clearly showed enhanced Ca++ activity relative to preparations that did not receive ETH1 (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ca++ imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: ETH1-induced Ca++ activity in VNC-Rk neurons can be divided into three principal phases.
claims.source: The traces could be divided into three principal phases, denoted with Arabic numbers to distinguish them from the behavioral phases, which we denote with Roman numerals.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of Ca++ imaging data.

claims.claim: Baseline Ca++ activity in VNC-Rk neurons rises over approximately the first 10-15 min after ETH1 addition (Phase 1).
claims.source: Typically, baseline Ca++ activity rose over approximately the first 10–15 min. after ETH1 addition (Figure 4, Phase 1), reached a peak during the next 20 min. (Phase 2), and then slowly declined (Phase 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of Ca++ imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Baseline Ca++ activity in VNC-Rk neurons reaches a peak during the next 20 min (Phase 2).
claims.source: Typically, baseline Ca++ activity rose over approximately the first 10–15 min. after ETH1 addition (Figure 4, Phase 1), reached a peak during the next 20 min. (Phase 2), and then slowly declined (Phase 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of Ca++ imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Baseline Ca++ activity in VNC-Rk neurons slowly declines during Phase 3.
claims.source: Typically, baseline Ca++ activity rose over approximately the first 10–15 min. after ETH1 addition (Figure 4, Phase 1), reached a peak during the next 20 min. (Phase 2), and then slowly declined (Phase 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of Ca++ imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Ca++ oscillations in VNC-Rk neurons initially exhibit relatively low amplitude and high frequency, but increase suddenly in amplitude during peak baseline activity in Phase 2.
claims.source: Superimposed on this baseline activity were Ca++ oscillations, which initially exhibited relatively low amplitude and high frequency, but which increased suddenly in amplitude during peak baseline activity in Phase 2.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of Ca++ imaging data.

claims.claim: After a transition period of mixed amplitude and frequency during the baseline decline in Phase 3, the oscillations slowed and became more uniformly large and regular.
claims.source: After a transition period of mixed amplitude and frequency during the baseline decline in Phase 3, the oscillations slowed and became more uniformly large and regular.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of Ca++ imaging data.

claims.claim: The phases of ETH1-induced Ca++ activity in VNC-Rk neurons have durations similar to the ecdysis behavioral phases observed in live animals.
claims.source: Consistent with the hypothesis that activity of the VNC-Rk neurons is correlated with the phases of the ecdysis motor programs, the phases of ETH1-induced Ca++ activity have durations similar to the ecdysis behavioral phases observed in live animals.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of Ca++ activity phase durations with behavioral phase durations.

claims.claim: The integrated Ca++ signal over the abdominal musculature in preparations expressing GCaMP6s in muscles exhibits a profile similar to that of the VNC-Rk neurons.
claims.source: The integrated Ca++ signal over the abdominal musculature in such preparations (dotted box) typically exhibited a profile similar to that of the VNC-Rk neurons and divided into three principal phases when processed using the PhaseFinder program.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of muscle Ca++ imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The average onset times of muscle Ca++ activity phases closely match those calculated for the three phases of VNC-Rk activity.
claims.source: The average onset times of these phases closely matched those calculated for the three phases of VNC-Rk activity by the same program (Figure 4C), again indicating a close correspondence between the neuronal activity and the three behavioral phases.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative comparison of phase onset times shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The transition of the VNC-Rk Ca++ activity from Phase 2 to Phase 3 is characterized by a variable interval with oscillations of mixed amplitude and frequency.
claims.source: As noted above, the transition of the VNC-Rk Ca++ activity from Phase 2 to Phase 3 is also characterized by a variable interval with oscillations of mixed amplitude and frequency.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of Ca++ imaging data.

claims.claim: An analogous transition period exists in the muscle Ca++ activity that corresponds to the interval of mixed behavior.
claims.source: To assess the similarity of this transition period to the observed interval of mixed behavior in the muscle Ca++ traces, we modified the PhaseFinder program to identify this transition period in the Phase III Ca++ data and found an analogous transition in the muscle Ca++ activity that corresponded to the interval of mixed behavior.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of muscle Ca++ imaging data using the PhaseFinder program.

claims.claim: The calculated durations of the transition periods in VNC-Rk neurons and muscle Ca++ activity were not significantly different.
claims.source: The calculated durations of the transition periods in the two experiments were not significantly different, although both exhibited a high degree of variation across preparations (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of transition period durations shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: VNC-Rk neuronal activity is correlated with the generation of the ecdysis motor programs.
claims.source: We interpret this additional, and initially unexpected, correspondence in the VNC-Rk and muscle Ca++ data as further evidence that VNC-Rk neuronal activity is correlated with the generation of the ecdysis motor programs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the multiple correspondences between neuronal and muscle Ca++ activity.

claims.claim: The characteristics of Ca++ signaling associated with each phase of VNC-Rk neuron activity differ from each other in ways similar to those of the ecdysis motor patterns.
claims.source: Further support for such a correlation comes from analyzing the spatiotemporal patterns of Ca++ signaling associated with each phase of VNC-Rk neuron activity, the characteristics of which differ from each other in ways similar to those of the ecdysis motor patterns (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of spatiotemporal patterns shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Left-right oscillations in the Phase 2 Ca++ signal of VNC-Rk neurons consistently oscillate in antiphase.
claims.source: These signals consistently oscillate in antiphase during Phase 2 (Pearson's correlation coefficient, R = −0.30 ± 0.13, p=0.0004, n = 8), but not, for example, during Phase 1, or the latter half of Phase 3 (Figure 5C, bottom) when the oscillations are coincident.
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of Ca++ signals shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Phase II muscle Ca++ activity is characterized by strong rhythmic activity alternating across the midline with robust, temporally anti-correlated peaks.
claims.source: The corresponding analysis of muscle-generated Ca++ signals shows that Phase II is similarly characterized by strong rhythmic activity alternating across the midline with robust, temporally anti-correlated peaks (R = −0.27 ± 0.213, p=0.0016, n = 11; Figure 5D,E).
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of muscle Ca++ signals shown in Figure 5D and E.

claims.claim: The frequencies of Phase 2 oscillations in VNC-Rk neurons (0.02 ± 0.05 Hz) and 24B muscles (0.03 ± 0.09 Hz) are similar.
claims.source: We found that both frequencies (0.02 ± 0.05 Hz for VNC-Rk neurons vs. 0.03 ± 0.09 Hz for 24B muscles) and oscillation numbers (23 ± 7 for VNC-Rk neurons vs. 18 ± 2 for 24B muscles) were similar.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of Ca++ oscillations.

claims.claim: The oscillation numbers in Phase 2 for VNC-Rk neurons (23 ± 7) and 24B muscles (18 ± 2) are similar.
claims.source: We found that both frequencies (0.02 ± 0.05 Hz for VNC-Rk neurons vs. 0.03 ± 0.09 Hz for 24B muscles) and oscillation numbers (23 ± 7 for VNC-Rk neurons vs. 18 ± 2 for 24B muscles) were similar.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of Ca++ oscillations.

claims.claim: Phase 2 activity of the VNC-Rk neurons drives the execution of the Phase II motor program.
claims.source: Taken together, these data are consistent with the hypothesis that Phase 2 activity of the VNC-Rk neurons drives the execution of the Phase II motor program.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between neuronal and muscle activity patterns.

claims.claim: The muscular activity responsible for the stretch compressions of Phase III exhibits bilaterally coincident peaks of Ca++ activity.
claims.source: In addition, the muscular activity responsible for the stretch compressions of Phase III exhibit bilaterally coincident peaks of Ca++ activity (R = 0.57 ± 0.14, p<0.0001, n = 11; Figure 5F, bottom traces), similar to those of VNC-Rk neuron activity during late Phase 3 (Figure 5C, bottom).
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of muscle Ca++ signals shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: VNC-Rk neuron activity during late Phase 3 exhibits bilaterally coincident peaks similar to Phase III muscle activity.
claims.source: In addition, the muscular activity responsible for the stretch compressions of Phase III exhibit bilaterally coincident peaks of Ca++ activity (R = 0.57 ± 0.14, p<0.0001, n = 11; Figure 5F, bottom traces), similar to those of VNC-Rk neuron activity during late Phase 3 (Figure 5C, bottom).
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The VNC-Rk population contains at least two types of neurons: one with large, slow changes in baseline amplitude and one with oscillatory activity but relatively constant baseline.
claims.source: Although we cannot be certain that these ROIs correspond to individual cells due to the limited resolution of the Ca++ signal in the z-dimension, their Ca++ activity traces fell into two broad categories: those with large, slow changes in baseline amplitude (i.e. #28, 84, 16), and those with oscillatory activity, but relatively constant baseline (i.e. #89, 2, 74). This suggests that the VNC-Rk population contains at least two types of neurons: one that may represent the oscillatory output of the network and one that may be involved in sustaining phasic activity within it.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of individual ROI Ca++ traces shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Approximately 10% of the VNC-Rk ROIs had frequency profiles similar to that of the global Ca++ trace.
claims.source: Analysis of the average frequency of oscillations as a function of phase for all 95 ROIs indicates that approximately 10% of the ROIs had frequency profiles similar to that of the global Ca++ trace (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Multifunctional neurons participate in the generation of all three phases of behavior.
claims.source: This observation is consistent with the conclusion that multifunctional neurons participate in the generation of all three phases of behavior, but more refined observation and manipulation of individual VNC-Rk neurons will be required to definitively determine their role(s) in central pattern generation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some ROIs show activity in multiple phases.

claims.claim: Rk-expressing neurons comprise a multifunctional central pattern generator (CPG) for the pupal ecdysis sequence.
claims.source: Overall, however, our analysis of the spatiotemporal structure of ETH1-induced Ca++ activity of the Rk-expressing neurons suggests that they comprise a multifunctional central pattern generator (CPG) for the pupal ecdysis sequence.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comprehensive analysis of Ca++ activity patterns.

claims.claim: Rk-expressing neurons communicate their output to downstream motor neurons.
claims.source: The hypothesis that Rk-expressing neurons act as central pattern generators for the ecdysis rhythms predicts that these neurons communicate their output to downstream motor neurons. To directly determine whether motor neurons receive input from Rk-expressing neurons, we used the ATP/P2X2 system to stimulate Rk-expressing neurons while monitoring the response of glutamatergic neurons in the VNC—95% of which are motor neurons (Daniels et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is tested experimentally using the ATP/P2X2 system.

claims.claim: 95% of glutamatergic neurons in the VNC are motor neurons.
claims.source: To directly determine whether motor neurons receive input from Rk-expressing neurons, we used the ATP/P2X2 system to stimulate Rk-expressing neurons while monitoring the response of glutamatergic neurons in the VNC—95% of which are motor neurons (Daniels et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Daniels et al., 2008.

claims.claim: ATP induces a substantial increase in Ca++ signal in a large number of glutamatergic neurons when Rk-expressing neurons are stimulated.
claims.source: We found that ATP induced a substantial increase in Ca++ signal in a large number of neurons (Figure 5G), indicating that glutamatergic motor neurons of the VNC are downstream targets of the Rk-expressing neurons.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ca++ imaging data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Glutamatergic motor neurons of the VNC are downstream targets of the Rk-expressing neurons.
claims.source: We found that ATP induced a substantial increase in Ca++ signal in a large number of neurons (Figure 5G), indicating that glutamatergic motor neurons of the VNC are downstream targets of the Rk-expressing neurons.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the Ca++ response of glutamatergic neurons to Rk neuron stimulation.

claims.claim: Very few CCAP-R-expressing neurons in the pupal CNS co-express either of the ETHR isoforms.
claims.source: We find that very few CCAP-R-expressing neurons in the pupal CNS co-express either of the ETHR isoforms, but that a significant complement are glutamatergic, as identified by the intersectional driver for CCAP-R and VGlut.
claims.evidence: This is supported by intersectional labeling data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A significant complement of CCAP-R-expressing neurons are glutamatergic.
claims.source: We find that very few CCAP-R-expressing neurons in the pupal CNS co-express either of the ETHR isoforms, but that a significant complement are glutamatergic, as identified by the intersectional driver for CCAP-R and VGlut.
claims.evidence: This is supported by intersectional labeling data.

claims.claim: Many of the glutamatergic neurons labeled by CCAP-R-P65AD ∩ vGlut-Gal4DBD are motor neurons, sending their axons out the abdominal nerves and forming synapses on muscles in the body wall.
claims.source: A fillet preparation of the pupal body wall in which the muscles are labeled with phalloidin (Figure 6A, magenta), reveals that many of the glutamatergic neurons labeled by UAS-6XGFP (Figure 6A, green), are motor neurons, sending their axons out the abdominal nerves and forming synapses on muscles in the body wall (Figure 6A', arrowheads).
claims.evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 6A and 6A'.

claims.claim: The profile of ETH1-induced Ca++ activity in CCAP-R/VGlut neurons is multiphasic and decomposes into three principal phases.
claims.source: Using the same intersectional driver to express UAS-GCaMP6s in these neurons (i.e. CCAP-R/VGlut neurons), we selectively monitored their response to ETH1 in excised pupal CNS preparations. Interestingly, the profile of the induced Ca++ activity is multiphasic and decomposes into three principal phases as distinguished by the PhaseFinder program (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ca++ imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The last phase of CCAP-R/VGlut neuron Ca++ activity contains an identifiable transition period with Ca++ oscillations of mixed amplitude and frequency.
claims.source: As for the Ca++ activity of the VNC-Rk neurons, the last phase contains an identifiable transition period with Ca++ oscillations of mixed amplitude and frequency, and the activity of Phase 2, when analyzed bilaterally across the midline, shows characteristic left-right alternations (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ca++ imaging data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claims.claim: Phase 2 activity of CCAP-R/VGlut neurons shows characteristic left-right alternations when analyzed bilaterally across the midline.
claims.source: As for the Ca++ activity of the VNC-Rk neurons, the last phase contains an identifiable transition period with Ca++ oscillations of mixed amplitude and frequency, and the activity of Phase 2, when analyzed bilaterally across the midline, shows characteristic left-right alternations (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ca++ imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The durations and frequencies of Ca++ activity for the CCAP-R/VGlut and VNC-Rk neurons were comparable, with no statistically significant differences found for any Phase.
claims.source: The durations (Figure 6D) and frequencies (Figure 6E) of Ca++ activity for the CCAP-R/VGlut and VNC-Rk neurons were comparable, with no statistically significant differences found for any Phase.
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of Ca++ activity parameters shown in Figure 6D and 6E.

claims.claim: The observations are consistent with a tight coupling between the activities of the VNC-Rk and CCAP-R/VGlut motor neurons.
claims.source: These observations are consistent with a tight coupling between the activities of the VNC-Rk and CCAP-R/VGlut motor neurons.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the similarity in Ca++ activity patterns.

claims.claim: Selective activation of the Rk-expressing neurons induces a large Ca++ response in the CCAP-R VNC neurons.
claims.source: To directly determine whether activity in CCAP-R neurons can be driven by the Rk-expressing neurons, we used the ATP/P2X2 system and found that selective activation of the Rk-expressing neurons induced a large Ca++ response in the CCAP-R VNC neurons (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ca++ imaging data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Motor neurons expressing the CCAP-R act downstream of CPG neurons that express the Bursicon receptor, Rickets.
claims.source: We conclude that motor neurons expressing the CCAP-R act downstream of CPG neurons that express the Bursicon receptor, Rickets.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the functional connectivity demonstrated by the ATP/P2X2 experiments.

claims.claim: Silencing the activity of ETHRB-expressing neurons with UAS-Kir2.1 causes a variety of behavioral defects, including rapid, tremulous movements of the body wall.
claims.source: Silencing the activity of ETHRB-expressing neurons with UAS-Kir2.1, caused a variety of behavioral defects, including rapid, tremulous movements of the body wall, but the most salient feature was the lack of an overt Phase I (Figure 7C; Video 8).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7C and Video 8.

claims.claim: The most salient feature of silencing ETHRB-expressing neurons is the lack of an overt Phase I.
claims.source: Silencing the activity of ETHRB-expressing neurons with UAS-Kir2.1, caused a variety of behavioral defects, including rapid, tremulous movements of the body wall, but the most salient feature was the lack of an overt Phase I (Figure 7C; Video 8).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7C and Video 8.

claims.claim: Phase II and Phase III motor programs are readily discernible in animals with silenced ETHRB-expressing neurons.
claims.source: Phase II and Phase III motor programs were readily discernible in affected animals, but the abdominal lifting which initiates Phase I was absent, and although some abdominal movements preceded Phase II, they appeared to be exaggerated versions of the body wall movements that normally prefigure the onset of Phase I, and they never displaced the abdominal air bubble as they do in normal animals.
claims.evidence: This is based on behavioral observations.

claims.claim: Animals in which the non-CCAP/ETHRA neurons were silenced exhibited obvious deficits in Phase I, which was consistently shorter than in controls.
claims.source: Animals in which the non-CCAP/ETHRA neurons were silenced also exhibited obvious deficits in Phase I, which was executed by most animals (n = 10/15), but was consistently shorter than it was in controls (3.82 ± 2.8 vs. 7.42 ± 3.5, p=0.0137; Figure 7D; Video 9).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7D and Video 9.

claims.claim: ETHRB and non-CCAP/ETHRA neurons have specific requirements in the initiation and maintenance of Phase I.
claims.source: These results indicate specific requirements for ETHRB and non-CCAP/ETHRA neurons in the initiation and maintenance of Phase I.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the behavioral deficits observed when these neurons are silenced.

claims.claim: Phase I was not induced by activating either ETHRB or non-CCAP/ETHRA neurons prior to the onset of ecdysis using UAS-TrpA1.
claims.source: Interestingly, Phase I was not induced by activating either of these populations of neurons prior to the onset of ecdysis using UAS-TrpA1, and further experiments will be required to identify the sufficient causes for initiation of this phase.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: The sites of action of the neuromodulators ETH, Bursicon, and CCAP identify essential functional components of the pupal ecdysis network architecture.
claims.source: Using the Trojan exon method to selectively target populations of hormone receptor-expressing neurons for manipulation and monitoring of activity, we have investigated the neuromodulatory connectivity of the circuitry governing pupal ecdysis behavior in Drosophila. We find that the sites of action of the neuromodulators ETH, Bursicon, and CCAP identify essential functional components of the network architecture, defining three hierarchically organized layers from the sites of hormonal initiation to the sites of motor neuron output.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claims.claim: The sites of action of ETH, Bursicon, and CCAP define three hierarchically organized layers from the sites of hormonal initiation to the sites of motor neuron output.
claims.source: We find that the sites of action of the neuromodulators ETH, Bursicon, and CCAP identify essential functional components of the network architecture, defining three hierarchically organized layers from the sites of hormonal initiation to the sites of motor neuron output.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claims.claim: Descending neuromodulatory signaling from the ETHR-expressing input layer governs the basic motor rhythms of the ecdysis sequence by modulating the intermediate CPG layer.
claims.source: In addition, we find that descending neuromodulatory signaling from the ETHR-expressing input layer not only governs the basic motor rhythms of the ecdysis sequence by modulating the intermediate CPG layer, but also modulates activity of the CCAP-R-expressing motor neurons of the output layer (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and summarized in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Descending neuromodulatory signaling from the ETHR-expressing input layer modulates activity of the CCAP-R-expressing motor neurons of the output layer.
claims.source: In addition, we find that descending neuromodulatory signaling from the ETHR-expressing input layer not only governs the basic motor rhythms of the ecdysis sequence by modulating the intermediate CPG layer, but also modulates activity of the CCAP-R-expressing motor neurons of the output layer (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and summarized in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Neuromodulators act broadly within, as well as across, network layers in the pupal ecdysis circuit.
claims.source: Neuromodulators thus act broadly within, as well as across, network layers.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that neuromodulators act at multiple levels of the network.

claims.claim: The functional architecture of the ecdysis network can be decoded from its patterns of neuromodulatory connectivity.
claims.source: Our finding that the functional architecture of the ecdysis network can be decoded from its patterns of neuromodulatory connectivity provides further evidence that characterizing neuromodulatory connectomes is a valuable strategy in elucidating neural networks.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claims.claim: Characterizing neuromodulatory connectomes is a valuable strategy in elucidating neural networks.
claims.source: Our finding that the functional architecture of the ecdysis network can be decoded from its patterns of neuromodulatory connectivity provides further evidence that characterizing neuromodulatory connectomes is a valuable strategy in elucidating neural networks.
claims.evidence: This is a general conclusion supported by the findings of this study.

claims.claim: The downstream targets of Bursicon and CCAP are shared components of the pupal ecdysis network and are used to generate all three motor rhythms.
claims.source: A principal finding reported here is that the downstream targets of Bursicon and CCAP are shared components of the pupal ecdysis network and are used to generate all three motor rhythms.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claims.claim: Neurons that express the Bursicon receptor (Rk) are absolutely required for all pupal ecdysis behavior.
claims.source: Our results draw particular attention to the centrality of neurons that express the Bursicon receptor (Rk), which are absolutely required for all pupal ecdysis behavior.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the suppression experiments showing complete loss of behavior.

claims.claim: A role in central pattern generation for VNC-Rk neurons is indicated both from the effects of their suppression and from their pattern of ETH1-induced Ca++ activity.
claims.source: A role in central pattern generation is indicated both from the effects of their suppression, which eliminates all motor activity, and from their pattern of ETH1-induced Ca++ activity, which matches the phases of ecdysis behavior.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the suppression and Ca++ imaging experiments.

claims.claim: ETH1-induced Ca++ activity in VNC-Rk neurons is centrally generated and observed in the absence of sensory feedback.
claims.source: The fact that ETH1-induced Ca++ activity is observed in the excised nervous system and thus in the absence of sensory feedback, demonstrates that it is centrally generated and further supports the identification of the VNC-Rk neurons as central pattern generators.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design using excised nervous systems.

claims.claim: The ecdysis circuitry includes multifunctional CPG neurons that express Rk and are subject to modulation by distinct input layer modules.
claims.source: However, our preliminary observation that regions containing at most small numbers of VNC-Rk neurons exhibit activity that is phasically coupled to two or more motor patterns argues that the ecdysis circuitry includes multifunctional CPG neurons that express Rk and are subject to modulation by distinct input layer modules, as indicated in Figure 7D.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of individual ROI activity patterns.

claims.claim: Direct activation of ETHRA/CCAP neurons induces Phase II-like rhythmic activity in the VNC-Rk neurons.
claims.source: Direct activation of these neurons induces Phase II-like rhythmic activity in the VNC-Rk neurons, an observation that is easily explained if Bursicon secreted from ETHRA/CCAP neurons shifts the mode of activity of the VNC-Rk CPG.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the ATP/P2X2 activation experiments.

claims.claim: Bursicon secreted from ETHRA/CCAP neurons shifts the mode of activity of the VNC-Rk CPG.
claims.source: Direct activation of these neurons induces Phase II-like rhythmic activity in the VNC-Rk neurons, an observation that is easily explained if Bursicon secreted from ETHRA/CCAP neurons shifts the mode of activity of the VNC-Rk CPG.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the activation experiments and is consistent with neuromodulatory control of CPGs.

claims.claim: The CCAP- and Bursicon-expressing neurons are known to express additional neuropeptides, including Myoinhibitory Peptides and Allatostatin C.
claims.source: The CCAP- and Bursicon-expressing neurons are known to express additional neuropeptides, including Myoinhibitory Peptides and Allatostatin C, and it is likely that these neuromodulators also play a role in regulating these phases.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the neuropeptide content of these neurons.

claims.claim: The mixed activity patterns that define the transition from Phase II to Phase III are readily interpreted as a period of bistability in which CPG modes transiently alternate.
claims.source: The mixed activity patterns that define the transition from Phase II to Phase III, first described by Kim et al. (2006) and further characterized here, are also readily interpreted as a period of bistability in which CPG modes transiently alternate, perhaps as Bursicon and/or other co-released neuromodulator concentrations fall.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed activity patterns, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The neurons that express the B-isoform of ETHR are required to initiate Phase I.
claims.source: Our results indicate that the largely uncharacterized neurons that express the B-isoform of ETHR are required to initiate Phase I, and that the non-CCAP/ETHRA neurons are important for maintaining that phase.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the suppression experiments showing loss of Phase I.

claims.claim: The non-CCAP/ETHRA neurons are important for maintaining Phase I.
claims.source: Our results indicate that the largely uncharacterized neurons that express the B-isoform of ETHR are required to initiate Phase I, and that the non-CCAP/ETHRA neurons are important for maintaining that phase.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the suppression experiments showing shortened Phase I.

claims.claim: The essential role of ETHRB-expressing neurons in Phase I initiation is consistent with the significantly higher affinity for ETH peptides of ETHRB compared with ETHRA.
claims.source: The essential role of ETHRB-expressing neurons in Phase I initiation is consistent with the significantly higher affinity for ETH peptides of ETHRB compared with ETHRA (Iversen et al., 2002; Park et al., 2003b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Iversen et al., 2002; Park et al., 2003b.

claims.claim: ETHRB-expressing neurons may initiate Phase I by responding to rising titers of ETH earlier than neurons expressing ETHRA.
claims.source: ETHRB-expressing neurons may thus initiate Phase I by responding to rising titers of ETH earlier than neurons expressing ETHRA.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the higher affinity of ETHRB for ETH.

claims.claim: The motor output of the pupal ecdysis network is mediated by neurons that express the CCAP-R.
claims.source: Our finding that the motor output of the pupal ecdysis network is mediated by neurons that express the CCAP-R provides insight into the hitherto poorly understood mechanism of action of CCAP.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the anatomical and functional data.

claims.claim: CCAP acts on motor neurons to render pupal ecdysis more robust.
claims.source: Our results indicate that it does so by acting on motor neurons, and because CCAP is co-released with Bursicon from the ETHRA/CCAP neurons to govern the CPG transition at Phase II, this suggests a role for feed-forward signaling in the pupal ecdysis circuit.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CCAP-R is expressed in motor neurons.

claims.claim: CCAP is co-released with Bursicon from the ETHRA/CCAP neurons to govern the CPG transition at Phase II.
claims.source: Our results indicate that it does so by acting on motor neurons, and because CCAP is co-released with Bursicon from the ETHRA/CCAP neurons to govern the CPG transition at Phase II, this suggests a role for feed-forward signaling in the pupal ecdysis circuit.
claims.evidence: This is based on prior knowledge and the current findings.

claims.claim: The architecture of the pupal ecdysis network revealed in this study is similar to that of other motor circuits governing locomotion, feeding, and breathing.
claims.source: The architecture of the pupal ecdysis network revealed here is similar to that of other motor circuits, such as those governing locomotion, feeding, and breathing in which higher order neurons modulate the activity of core CPGs to generate varied motor patterns (Feldman et al., 2013; Mullins et al., 2011; Nusbaum et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to other systems, supported by citations.

claims.claim: ETH acts throughout the input layer to control different phases of pupal ecdysis behavior.
claims.source: What is striking about neuromodulator action in the ecdysis circuit is its broad scope. ETH acts throughout the input layer to control different phases of pupal ecdysis behavior; Bursicon similarly regulates a large and essential set of neurons constituting the ecdysis CPG; and CCAP acts on many motor neurons necessary for generating the rhythmic ecdysis movements.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings about ETH action.

claims.claim: Bursicon regulates a large and essential set of neurons constituting the ecdysis CPG.
claims.source: What is striking about neuromodulator action in the ecdysis circuit is its broad scope. ETH acts throughout the input layer to control different phases of pupal ecdysis behavior; Bursicon similarly regulates a large and essential set of neurons constituting the ecdysis CPG; and CCAP acts on many motor neurons necessary for generating the rhythmic ecdysis movements.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings about Bursicon action.

claims.claim: CCAP acts on many motor neurons necessary for generating the rhythmic ecdysis movements.
claims.source: What is striking about neuromodulator action in the ecdysis circuit is its broad scope. ETH acts throughout the input layer to control different phases of pupal ecdysis behavior; Bursicon similarly regulates a large and essential set of neurons constituting the ecdysis CPG; and CCAP acts on many motor neurons necessary for generating the rhythmic ecdysis movements.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings about CCAP action.

claims.claim: Bursicon and CCAP signal from the input layer to provide coherence to the operation of the pupal ecdysis network by acting both within each hierarchical layer and by acting coordinately across layers.
claims.source: The observation that Bursicon and CCAP signal from the input layer speaks to an organizational logic in which the ecdysial neuromodulators function together to provide coherence to the operation of the pupal ecdysis network by acting both within each hierarchical layer and by acting coordinately across layers.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the organizational logic inferred from the findings.

claims.claim: This organization is consistent with a generalized role for neuromodulatory systems in organizing neural activity to generate behavior.
claims.source: This organization is consistent with a generalized role for neuromodulatory systems in organizing neural activity to generate behavior (Marder, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a general conclusion supported by the findings and a citation to Marder, 2012.

claims.claim: Mapping of the pupal ecdysis network was done without reference to patterns of synaptic connectivity.
claims.source: It is worth noting that our mapping of the pupal ecdysis network was done without reference to patterns of synaptic connectivity.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the methodology used in the study.

claims.claim: Synaptic connectomes have proved difficult to interpret, in part due to their dense interconnectivity.
claims.source: Synaptic connectomes have proved difficult to interpret, in part due to their dense interconnectivity.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about the challenges of interpreting synaptic connectomes.

claims.claim: Dense interconnectivity in synaptic connectomes may reflect the multifunctionality of the underlying networks.
claims.source: If, as has been previously emphasized (Bargmann and Marder, 2013; Brezina, 2010; Marder, 2012), this interconnectivity reflects the multifunctionality of the underlying networks, and if the functional configuration of a network at any given time is determined by where and how neuromodulators are acting on its components, then patterns of neuromodulatory connectivity may provide a necessary complement to synaptic maps to render them interpretable.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claims.claim: Patterns of neuromodulatory connectivity may provide a necessary complement to synaptic maps to render them interpretable.
claims.source: If, as has been previously emphasized (Bargmann and Marder, 2013; Brezina, 2010; Marder, 2012), this interconnectivity reflects the multifunctionality of the underlying networks, and if the functional configuration of a network at any given time is determined by where and how neuromodulators are acting on its components, then patterns of neuromodulatory connectivity may provide a necessary complement to synaptic maps to render them interpretable.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations and the findings of this study.

claims.claim: When critical neuromodulator systems are known, the neuromodulatory connections can deliver substantial insight into how a neural network is organized.
claims.source: A key challenge will lie in identifying which neuromodulator systems play critical roles in establishing a network's output, but as the work here demonstrates, when these are known, the neuromodulatory connections can deliver substantial insight into how a neural network is organized.
claims.evidence: This is a general conclusion supported by the findings of this study.

results.result: ETHRA/CCAP neurons are necessary and sufficient for Phase I termination and Phase II initiation. Chronic suppression of these neurons blocks Phase II and III execution and extends Phase I duration, while activation terminates Phase I and initiates Phase II, followed by Phase III execution.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C58 collectively demonstrate through suppression (C50-C52) and activation (C54-C56) experiments that ETHRA/CCAP neurons control phase transitions. The data from Figure 1 showing behavioral effects of neuronal manipulation with Kir2.1 and dTrpA1 provide strong converging evidence for necessity and sufficiency.

results.result: CCAP and Bursicon act synergistically to mediate signaling by ETHRA/CCAP neurons. Double mutants lacking both CCAP and Pburs show severe Phase II deficits (70-90% fail head eversion), while single mutants show relatively normal or partially rescued phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 demonstrate synergistic hormone action through genetic epistasis analysis. The comparison of single versus double mutant phenotypes (C61-C63) provides strong evidence for synergy, supported by citation to Lahr et al., 2012.

results.result: Rk and CCAP-R are expressed in almost completely distinct neuronal populations in the CNS at pupal ecdysis. Few neurons co-express both receptors, indicating that Bursicon and CCAP synergy does not result from convergence on common targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C67 are supported by intersectional labeling data in Figure 2A showing minimal overlap between Rk and CCAP-R expression patterns. The inference that synergy is not due to common targets (C67) logically follows from the anatomical data.

results.result: Neurons expressing Rk or CCAP-R are both essential for pupal ecdysis, with distinct phenotypes upon suppression. Rk neuron suppression eliminates all movement while CCAP-R neuron suppression produces weak, irregular contractions resembling Phase I.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C74 are supported by suppression experiments shown in Figure 2B-C and Video 3. The complete loss of movement with Rk suppression (C70) versus partial activity with CCAP-R suppression (C73) demonstrates distinct functional roles for these populations.

results.result: Rk-expressing neurons occupy an intermediate position in the circuit hierarchy, as they are not motor neurons (lack VGlut co-expression and muscle projections) and do not highly co-express ETHR isoforms (input layer markers).
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78 are supported by intersectional labeling data in Figure 3A showing minimal overlap between Rk and VGlut or ETHR markers. The inference of intermediate circuit position (C78) logically follows from exclusion from input and output layers.

results.result: ATP-induced activation of Bursicon-expressing neurons produces alternating left-right oscillations in VNC-Rk neurons lasting ~9 minutes with ~15 cycles, resembling the Phase II swinging motor program (~18 bouts, ~17 minutes).
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C83 are supported by Ca++ imaging data in Figure 3B-C showing ATP-induced oscillatory activity. The correlation between neuronal activity patterns and behavioral motor output (C81-C83) is well-supported by quantitative similarity in duration and cycle number.

results.result: ETH1 induces phasic Ca++ activity in VNC-Rk neurons that can be divided into three principal phases with durations similar to behavioral ecdysis phases. Baseline activity rises over 10-15 min (Phase 1), peaks for ~20 min (Phase 2), then declines (Phase 3), with superimposed oscillations that change in amplitude and frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C92 are supported by Ca++ imaging data in Figure 4A showing ETH1-induced multiphasic activity. The correspondence between neuronal activity phase durations and behavioral phase durations (C92) is supported by quantitative comparison using the PhaseFinder program.

results.result: Muscle Ca++ activity during pupal ecdysis exhibits a profile similar to VNC-Rk neuron activity, with three principal phases whose onset times closely match those of VNC-Rk activity. Both show a transition period with mixed oscillations between Phases 2 and 3.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 are supported by muscle Ca++ imaging data in Figure 4B-C showing parallel phase structure. The close temporal correspondence between neuronal and muscle activity (C94) and similar transition periods (C96-C97) provide strong evidence for correlation.

results.result: Phase 2 activity of VNC-Rk neurons shows left-right alternating oscillations (R=-0.30, p=0.0004) that correlate with Phase II muscle activity (R=-0.27, p=0.0016). Oscillation frequencies (0.02 vs 0.03 Hz) and numbers (23 vs 18) are similar between neurons and muscles.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C104 are supported by spatiotemporal analysis in Figure 5 showing anti-correlated bilateral oscillations. Statistical correlation analysis (C100-C101) and quantitative comparison of frequencies and cycle numbers (C102-C103) provide strong evidence that VNC-Rk Phase 2 activity drives Phase II motor output.

results.result: Phase III muscle activity and late Phase 3 VNC-Rk neuron activity both exhibit bilaterally coincident Ca++ peaks (muscle R=0.57, p<0.0001), contrasting with the anti-phase oscillations of Phase II.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C106 are supported by correlation analysis in Figure 5C and 5F showing in-phase bilateral activity during Phase III. The statistical significance (p<0.0001) and contrast with Phase II anti-phase activity provide strong evidence.

results.result: VNC-Rk neurons comprise a multifunctional central pattern generator with at least two neuron types: those with large baseline changes and those with oscillatory activity. Approximately 10% of ROIs show frequency profiles similar to the global signal, suggesting multifunctional neurons participate in all three behavioral phases.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C110 are supported by single-ROI analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing heterogeneous activity patterns. However, the authors acknowledge limitations in z-resolution and note that definitive determination of individual neuron roles requires further work, tempering the strength of this conclusion.

results.result: Rk-expressing neurons communicate with downstream glutamatergic motor neurons. ATP-induced activation of Rk neurons produces substantial Ca++ increases in VGlut-expressing neurons (95% of which are motor neurons).
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C114 are supported by ATP/P2X2 activation experiments shown in Figure 5G. The functional connectivity is demonstrated by Ca++ response in glutamatergic neurons upon Rk neuron stimulation, with the motor neuron identity supported by citation to Daniels et al., 2008.

results.result: CCAP-R-expressing neurons include glutamatergic motor neurons that project axons to body wall muscles and form neuromuscular synapses. Few CCAP-R neurons co-express ETHR isoforms, but a significant complement are glutamatergic.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 are supported by intersectional labeling and anatomical data in Figure 6A showing CCAP-R/VGlut neurons with axonal projections to muscles. The identification of neuromuscular synapses (arrowheads in Figure 6A') provides strong anatomical evidence.

results.result: CCAP-R/VGlut motor neurons show multiphasic ETH1-induced Ca++ activity similar to VNC-Rk neurons, with three phases including a transition period and Phase 2 left-right alternations. Phase durations and frequencies are statistically indistinguishable between the two populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C122 are supported by Ca++ imaging data in Figure 6B-E showing parallel activity patterns. Statistical comparison (C121) demonstrates no significant differences in phase durations or frequencies, supporting tight coupling between CPG and motor neurons (C122).

results.result: Motor neurons expressing CCAP-R act downstream of CPG neurons expressing the Bursicon receptor Rk. Selective ATP-induced activation of Rk neurons produces large Ca++ responses in CCAP-R VNC neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C124 are supported by ATP/P2X2 experiments shown in Figure 6F demonstrating functional connectivity. The directional inference (C124) is supported by the hierarchical organization established through prior anatomical and functional data.

results.result: ETHRB-expressing neurons are required to initiate Phase I, while non-CCAP/ETHRA neurons are important for maintaining Phase I. Silencing ETHRB neurons eliminates overt Phase I but preserves Phases II and III; silencing non-CCAP/ETHRA neurons shortens Phase I (3.82±2.8 vs 7.42±3.5 min, p=0.0137).
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C130 are supported by suppression experiments in Figure 7C-D and Videos 8-9. The distinct phenotypes (complete loss vs. shortening of Phase I) demonstrate specific roles for these neuronal populations. However, activation experiments failed to induce Phase I (C130), indicating necessity but not sufficiency.

results.result: The sites of action of ETH, Bursicon, and CCAP define three hierarchically organized layers of the pupal ecdysis network: input layer (ETHR-expressing), CPG layer (Rk-expressing), and motor output layer (CCAP-R-expressing). Neuromodulators act both within and across these layers.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C135 represent the main conclusion synthesizing all experimental findings. The hierarchical organization is supported by anatomical data (receptor expression patterns), functional data (suppression/activation experiments), and connectivity data (ATP/P2X2 experiments). The comprehensive evidence across multiple experimental approaches strongly supports this network architecture.

results.result: The functional architecture of the ecdysis network can be decoded from patterns of neuromodulatory connectivity, demonstrating that characterizing neuromodulatory connectomes is a valuable strategy for elucidating neural networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C137 represent the overarching conclusion about methodology. The successful mapping of network architecture through neuromodulatory connectivity (without requiring synaptic connectivity data) provides proof-of-principle for this approach, supported by the comprehensive experimental results.

results.result: The downstream targets of Bursicon and CCAP are shared components used to generate all three motor rhythms. Rk-expressing neurons are absolutely required for all pupal ecdysis behavior and function as multifunctional CPG neurons subject to modulation by distinct input layer modules.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C142 synthesize findings about CPG organization. The requirement for Rk neurons across all phases (C139) is demonstrated by complete loss of movement upon suppression. The CPG role (C140-C141) is supported by suppression effects and centrally-generated activity patterns. The multifunctional nature (C142) is supported by ROI analysis, though the authors note this requires further validation.

results.result: Direct activation of ETHRA/CCAP neurons induces Phase II-like rhythmic activity in VNC-Rk neurons, consistent with Bursicon secretion shifting the mode of activity of the VNC-Rk CPG.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C144 are supported by ATP/P2X2 activation experiments. The observation of Phase II-like activity (C143) is demonstrated experimentally, and the mechanistic interpretation involving Bursicon-mediated CPG mode switching (C144) is a reasonable inference consistent with neuromodulatory control principles.

results.result: The mixed activity patterns defining the transition from Phase II to Phase III represent a period of bistability in which CPG modes transiently alternate, possibly as Bursicon and/or co-released neuromodulator concentrations fall.
results.evaluation: Claim C146 provides a mechanistic interpretation of the transition period observed in both neuronal and muscle Ca++ data. The bistability interpretation is consistent with the mixed oscillation patterns documented in Figures 4-5 and is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2006, though direct measurement of neuromodulator concentrations is not provided.

results.result: ETHRB-expressing neurons initiate Phase I, possibly by responding to rising ETH titers earlier than ETHRA neurons due to ETHRB's higher affinity for ETH peptides. Non-CCAP/ETHRA neurons maintain Phase I.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C148 are supported by suppression experiments in Figure 7. The mechanistic explanation based on receptor affinity differences (C149-C150) is supported by citations to Iversen et al., 2002 and Park et al., 2003b, providing a plausible molecular basis for the observed functional differences.

results.result: The motor output of the pupal ecdysis network is mediated by CCAP-R-expressing neurons. CCAP acts on motor neurons to render pupal ecdysis more robust, and is co-released with Bursicon from ETHRA/CCAP neurons, suggesting feedforward signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C153 are supported by anatomical identification of CCAP-R motor neurons (Figure 6A) and functional data showing their requirement for ecdysis. The feedforward signaling interpretation (C152-C153) is a reasonable inference from the co-release of CCAP and Bursicon acting on different layers, though direct demonstration of feedforward effects is not provided.

results.result: The architecture of the pupal ecdysis network is similar to other motor circuits governing locomotion, feeding, and breathing, where higher order neurons modulate core CPG activity to generate varied motor patterns.
results.evaluation: Claim C154 places the findings in broader context through comparison to other motor systems. The comparison is supported by citations to Feldman et al., 2013; Mullins et al., 2011; Nusbaum et al., 2001, demonstrating that the hierarchical organization observed here is a common motif in motor control.

results.result: Neuromodulator action in the ecdysis circuit has broad scope: ETH acts throughout the input layer, Bursicon regulates the CPG, and CCAP acts on motor neurons. Bursicon and CCAP signal from the input layer to provide coherence by acting within and across hierarchical layers, consistent with a generalized organizational role for neuromodulatory systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C159 synthesize findings about neuromodulatory organization. The broad scope of action (C155-C157) is demonstrated by the expression patterns and functional requirements. The organizational logic (C158) is a reasonable inference from the data, and the generalization to neuromodulatory systems (C159) is supported by citation to Marder, 2012.

results.result: Mapping the pupal ecdysis network without synaptic connectivity data demonstrates that patterns of neuromodulatory connectivity may complement synaptic maps to render them interpretable, particularly for multifunctional networks. When critical neuromodulator systems are known, neuromodulatory connections deliver substantial insight into network organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C164 present the methodological implications. The successful network mapping without synaptic data (C160) is demonstrated by the study. The hypothesis that neuromodulatory connectivity complements synaptic maps (C163) is supported by citations to Bargmann and Marder, 2013; Brezina, 2010; Marder, 2012, and the current findings provide empirical support for this approach.

results.result: Neural networks are typically defined by synaptic connectivity, yet synaptic wiring diagrams often provide limited insight into network function, partly due to the importance of non-synaptic neuromodulatory communication that can dynamically reconfigure circuit activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 establish the conceptual framework and motivation for the study. These are well-established principles in neuroscience supported by general knowledge and the broader literature, setting up the rationale for focusing on neuromodulatory connectivity.

results.result: The pupal ecdysis sequence in Drosophila is governed by serial release of factors (ETH, EH, CCAP, Bursicon) that act as both hormones and neuromodulators. The neuronal targets of these factors define hierarchically organized network layers (input, CPG, motor output), and mapping neuromodulatory connections defines the functional architecture.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C9 present the abstract/introduction summary of the study's approach and main findings. These claims are supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, representing the study's central thesis validated by the results.

results.result: Neuromodulators act at virtually all levels of sensorimotor processing to tune neuronal properties, profoundly influencing circuit function. They may coordinate activity in broadly distributed circuits over long timescales and distances, suggesting that identifying sites of neuromodulator action is a productive strategy for mapping critical circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C15 establish the theoretical background from prior literature. These are well-supported by citations to Marder, 2012; Nadim and Bucher, 2014; van den Pol, 2012; Bargmann, 2012; and others. The methodological hypothesis (C15) is tested and validated by the current study.

results.result: Historical observations showed that brain-derived hormones and biogenic amines induce complex motor programs, including moth emergence, egg-laying, and postural changes. Octopamine acts as an insect locomotor activator and modulates muscle metabolism and visual processing during flight.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C20 provide historical context supported by citations to classic studies (Harris-Warrick, 1988; Truman and Riddiford, 1970; Kupfermann, 1967; Livingstone et al., 1980; Libersat and Pflueger, 2004; Suver et al., 2012). These establish precedent for the neuromodulator mapping approach.

results.result: The crustacean stomatogastric ganglion contains two CPGs (pyloric and gastric mill) that are reconfigured by neuromodulators. Proctolin and CabTRP, co-released from MCN1, activate the same current but have different effects because they target distinct cells within the CPGs, coordinating changes in functionally related circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C29 describe the STG system as a precedent for neuromodulatory circuit organization. All claims are supported by citations to Marder and Bucher, 2007; Blitz et al., 1999; Swensen and Marder, 2000; Wood et al., 2000; Beenhakker and Nusbaum, 2004; Blitz et al., 2004, establishing the conceptual framework for the current study.

results.result: Cross-species differences in striatal vasopressin receptor expression in vole species correlate with and cause monogamous versus polygamous mating predispositions. Variations in neuromodulator receptor expression during speciation have been proposed as a major driver of behavioral evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32 provide examples of neuromodulator receptor expression influencing behavior, supported by citations to Hammock and Young, 2005; Young et al., 1997; Katz and Lillvis, 2014. These establish the broader significance of mapping neuromodulator receptor expression patterns.

results.result: Conserved neuromodulators like oxytocin and NPY regulate distinct circuits promoting specific behaviors (social recognition, pup retrieval, social learning, feeding) across multiple species, demonstrating that neuromodulators coordinate activity in broadly distributed circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 provide contemporary examples of neuromodulatory circuit organization, supported by citations to Ferguson et al., 2001; Marlin et al., 2015; Choe et al., 2015; Taghert and Nitabach, 2012. These establish the relevance and generality of the neuromodulatory mapping approach.

results.result: Molting in insects is accomplished by an ecdysis sequence initiated by ETH release, which facilitates secretion of EH, CCAP, and Bursicon. In Drosophila pupal ecdysis, three behavioral phases are characterized by distinct motor rhythms, with Phase II specifically dependent on CCAP and Bursicon from ETH-targeted neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C46 establish the biological system being studied, supported by citations to White and Ewer, 2014; Diao et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2006; Mena et al., 2016; Lahr et al., 2012. These provide essential background on the ecdysis system and prior knowledge about its hormonal control.

results.result: A subset of CCAP-expressing neurons (ETHRA/CCAP neurons) expresses ETHRA and is required for head eversion during Phase II of pupal ecdysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48 cite prior work from the same laboratory (Diao et al., 2016) establishing the ETHRA/CCAP neuron population. This provides the starting point for the current investigation into downstream targets.

results.result: CCAP- and Bursicon-expressing neurons are known to express additional neuropeptides including Myoinhibitory Peptides and Allatostatin C, which likely also play roles in regulating ecdysis phases.
results.evaluation: Claim C145 acknowledges additional complexity in the system based on established knowledge about neuropeptide co-expression. This is a reasonable caveat noting that the study focuses on CCAP and Bursicon but other co-released factors may contribute.
